stories.author: mara-voss

articles.title: Saffron finishes the job, ends Mossdeep’s perfect season and wins the Indigo Bowl
articles.dek: HeeDee Lamb’s 153 receiving yards and NeMarcus Tare’s four sacks help the Psi Corps win 24–17 after Mossdeep loses Accel BeckhmJr in the first quarter.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Saffron had already watched Mossdeep turn a halftime deficit into a win once this season. At Indigo Plateau, the Psi Corps answered every attempt to do it again. Archam Manning threw for 337 yards, HeeDee Lamb supplied the biggest receiving afternoon of the final, and NeMarcus Tare kept appearing in the backfield when the Eclipse needed a clean possession. Saffron won the Indigo Bowl 24–17, completing a four-win postseason and handing Mossdeep its first defeat in twenty games.

The Eclipse lost Accel BeckhmJr in the first quarter and finished the first half without a point. The league’s eventual MVP caught one pass for ten yards. Two first-half turnovers ended Mossdeep scoring chances in the red zone, leaving a team that had scored 724 regular-season points trying to climb back from 10–0 without its most decorated receiver. It climbed far enough to make Saffron recover an onside kick. It never led.

Trent Scarboro’s champions finished 18–3 overall. Michael Dorrill’s Eclipse finished 19–1, with a conference title and a final that will occupy an unreasonable amount of the coach’s offseason. The statistical margins were small enough to make the lost opportunities hurt: sixteen first downs apiece, Saffron ahead 403–373 in total yards, and only two more offensive plays for the Psi Corps. The turnovers were entirely Mossdeep’s. So was the burden of needing one more possession at the end.
Tare and Farris interrupt the opening challenge

Mossdeep forced a punt on Saffron’s first series. Tare then sacked Dram Marino on the Eclipse’s first offensive snap, beginning a four-sack afternoon with a seven-yard loss. Marino found BeckhmJr for ten yards on the next play, and the offense worked out of the hole. Ninjaskamara gained thirteen on third-and-seven, then nine more on the following run. Ninjulio Jones and Shawn Mareman helped keep the possession moving.

Fliff Farris ended it. On second-and-five, Marino’s deep pass to the right was intercepted and returned sixteen yards. Saffron took over and constructed the game’s first touchdown drive: thirteen plays, eighty yards, and enough answers after difficult downs to establish how this final would be played.

Manning found Lamb for twenty-five on third-and-eight. Joey Sporeter subsequently sacked Manning, but Dam Skattebo gained eleven on third-and-thirteen and Lamb caught a short pass for ten on fourth-and-two. Those were useful, expensive conversions. Mossdeep had created the situations it wanted and still had to keep defending. The drive crossed into the second quarter, ending with Skattebo’s two-yard touchdown run on the snap at 5:20.

“We kept giving ourselves another down,” Manning said. “The sack doesn’t get to decide the entire drive. Somebody still has a route to run, and somebody still has a block to finish.” His calm explanation matched an afternoon in which he completed twenty-one of twenty-nine passes and threw no interception despite being sacked three times.
A second turnover leaves Mossdeep empty at halftime

The teams exchanged punts before Mossdeep assembled a nine-play, sixty-four-yard possession. The Eclipse again moved into position to score. On the snap at 1:00, Marino completed a short pass to Ninjaskamara for ten yards. Ninjaskamara fumbled, and Pach Tatum recovered for Saffron. Mossdeep’s first-half work had produced two turnovers and no points.

Saffron used the remaining time aggressively. Manning hit Lamb for twenty-five and thirty-two yards, with an incompletion between those gains, then found Mothel Irving for eighteen. Pawmo and Skattebo advanced the ball further before Octillery made a nineteen-yard field goal on the snap at eleven seconds. The recorded drive covered ninety-six yards. Instead of closing the gap before halftime, Mossdeep watched it grow to ten.

“We moved it and gave it away,” Dorrill said. “Nobody needs a presentation to understand that. We had possessions we could finish, and we didn’t finish them. Losing a player changes your assignments. It doesn’t excuse the ball coming out.”

BeckhmJr’s absence changed the receiving work substantially. Derrat Brooks, the All-League linebacker, finished with five catches for ninety-four yards on nine targets. Ninjulio caught four for eighty-four. The game asked Mossdeep to find production in unfamiliar places, and it found some. Replacing an MVP’s opportunities while trailing in a championship remained a difficult way to spend the afternoon.

body.alt: An imagined Indigo Plateau stadium from high in the stands, with a bright field framed by distant mountain ridges.
body.caption: An imagined view of the neutral-site Indigo Bowl at Indigo Plateau.

body.text: Every Mossdeep score receives a Saffron answer

Mossdeep opened the second half with its best sustained possession: twelve plays and seventy-nine yards. Tare’s third sack pushed the Eclipse into third-and-fourteen, but Marino found Ninjulio for twenty-six. Ninjaskamara contributed as both runner and receiver before Driflon Diggs caught the six-yard touchdown pass on third-and-two. Adam Vinathorn’s extra point cut the lead to 10–7.

Saffron immediately went seventy-eight yards in eight plays. Ray Glewis sacked Manning, and the Psi Corps again faced a difficult series of downs. Gengar Pickens caught fourteen yards on third-and-sixteen and nine more on fourth-and-two. Irving added twenty-two. Then Lamb caught Manning’s deep-right pass for a thirty-seven-yard touchdown on the snap at 1:03 of the third quarter. The extra point restored a ten-point lead.

Lamb finished with seven catches for 153 yards and the touchdown, earning Player of the Game. His earlier catches had kept the first touchdown drive alive and supplied fifty-seven yards on the late first-half field-goal possession. He was involved in the practical work of maintaining the lead as well as its most spectacular extension.

“You don’t need every catch to be the one everybody remembers,” Lamb said. “That fourth down early mattered. Getting us moving before the half mattered. Archam gave me chances to keep those possessions going.”

Vinathorn’s thirty-five-yard field goal early in the fourth quarter brought Mossdeep within 17–10. Saffron answered again. Sporeter opened the next drive with another sack; Skattebo responded with a twelve-yard run. Pickens converted third-and-two, then later third-and-three with a twenty-nine-yard catch. Pawmo finished the seventy-eight-yard drive by catching a seven-yard touchdown pass. With the extra point, Saffron led 24–10.

body.alt: A painted American football follows a single arc over the right side of a stylized field.
body.caption: Archam Manning went deep right to HeeDee Lamb for a 37-yard touchdown with 1:03 left in the third quarter. The flight path is illustrative.

body.text: The final chance ends at the onside kick

Tare’s fourth sack arrived on Mossdeep’s next possession. Marino eventually completed fourteen yards to Ninjulio on fourth-and-seventeen, leaving the Eclipse short and giving Saffron another chance to end the contest. The Psi Corps reached the Mossdeep red zone, but Gyarls Woodson stopped Skattebo for no gain on fourth-and-four. Mossdeep took over with 1:09 showing before its next snap.

Marino drove the Eclipse ninety-six yards in nine plays. Brooks caught passes for sixteen and twenty-one yards; Ninjaskamara gained thirty-two through the air. With two spikes keeping the clock manageable, Marino found Ninjaskamara for the fourteen-yard touchdown on the snap at twenty seconds. Vinathorn’s extra point made it 24–17.

The final requirement was an onside recovery. Vinathorn’s kick was recovered by Saffron’s Crustle at the Mossdeep forty-nine. Manning knelt once. Scarboro’s team had secured the last onside kick and completed a postseason that ran through Olivine, Lavender, Mt. Silver and the unbeaten Eclipse.

“They kept coming,” Scarboro said. “That’s a nineteen-win team, and you felt it right through the last kick. Our guys had to earn the next possession, the next stop, the next recovery. I’m proud of every one of them.”

Marino finished 17-of-27 for 277 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. Ninjaskamara added fifty-four rushing yards and seventy-two receiving yards. For Saffron, Pickens caught all six of his targets for eighty-four yards, while Skattebo contributed fifty rushing yards and the first touchdown. Tare supplied all four Saffron sacks. When Mossdeep needed an improbable extra possession, Crustle secured the ball that denied it.

articles.title: Accel BeckhmJr wins MVP as Mossdeep and Saffron dominate the official honors
articles.dek: The complete individual awards and both All-League teams, plus a reckoning for PSPN’s six saved ballots.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Accel BeckhmJr won the league’s Most Valuable Player and Offensive Player of the Year awards with a regular season that deserves to be described before the injury that ended his championship afternoon. He caught 79 passes for 1,953 yards and 32 touchdowns in fifteen appearances. The receiving-yard lead over HeeDee Lamb was 75. The receiving-touchdown lead was fourteen. Mossdeep’s receiver produced a scoring season nobody else approached.

The final supplied a painful juxtaposition: the league’s most decorated offensive player left in the first quarter of a seven-point loss. His awards recognize the regular season. They do not become less deserved because Saffron won the Indigo Bowl, and NeMarcus Tare’s Defensive Player of the Year award does not need his four sacks in the final to explain it. Tare already led the league with 29 regular-season sacks in thirteen appearances.

Mossdeep also supplied Coach of the Year Michael Dorrill and eleven All-League selections, eight on the first team. Saffron had seven selections, three on the first team. Both finalists had exceptional seasons before they met at Indigo Plateau. The official honors show the breadth of the Eclipse’s achievement and the quality of the opponent that finally beat them.
BeckhmJr’s scoring lead wins the argument

I voted for Dram Marino as MVP and BeckhmJr as Offensive Player of the Year. Marino’s 56 touchdown passes and four interceptions were my reason for separating those ballots. The official result asks me to take another look at how much of the quarterback’s extraordinary scoring rate came through the receiver who scored 32 receiving touchdowns. BeckhmJr’s case was available all along; four of us selected him as the league’s best offensive player. None of us took the next step on the MVP ballot.

Marino finished with 4,341 passing yards. Archam Manning led the league with 4,633, and Rowan Vale preferred him for MVP. Dorian Pike chose Garshawn Lynch, whose 1,200 rushing yards came in eleven appearances. Those were serious candidates. BeckhmJr’s advantage was the combination of yardage leadership and an enormous scoring gap at his position. Thirty-two receiving touchdowns on 79 catches is a touchdown on more than two of every five receptions.

The playoff totals belong in a separate sentence: twelve catches, 247 yards and three touchdowns across three games. The final accounts for just one catch and ten yards. That absence was devastating to Mossdeep’s last game; the preceding season explains why.
Tare leads a championship pass rush

Tare’s 29 regular-season sacks came with 65 pressures, 37 tackles, five non-sack tackles for loss, twelve passes defended and an interception. Saffron teammate Chen Norton Jr finished second in sacks with 23. An opponent preparing for the Psi Corps had to account for two established threats at once, and Tare still led the league despite appearing in thirteen games.

He added fourteen sacks and 28 pressures in four playoff games. Those numbers help describe Saffron’s championship run, while the regular-season line explains the award itself. His four sacks against Mossdeep included a seven-yard loss on the Eclipse’s opening offensive snap and another on the failed fourth-quarter series. A league award and a championship performance can reinforce each other without confusing which games were judged.

Five of our six writers chose Tare. Dorian preferred Blayz Matthews, whose 17.5 sacks and seventy pressures gave him a defensible pressure-based argument. The difference between the two seasons becomes clear when the quarterback actually went down: Tare finished 11.5 sacks ahead.
Ponyta and Volbeat win the rookie honors

Veilstone’s Ponyta won Offensive Rookie of the Year with 48 catches for 750 yards and five receiving touchdowns in fifteen appearances. The receiver also contributed 292 return yards. Viridian’s Dragonair finished fifteen receiving yards behind, close enough to explain Calvin Rook’s vote. Veilstone teammate Vigoroth rushed for 807 yards and received Ellis Quill’s ballot. Veilstone has two young offensive contributors to build around even after a six-win season.

Mauville’s Volbeat won Defensive Rookie of the Year after thirteen sacks, 43 tackles, seven non-sack tackles for loss, 23 pressures and six passes defended. Cinnabar’s Tatsugiri supplied the strongest competing coverage argument: 81 tackles, five interceptions and thirteen passes defended, plus a first-team All-League selection. Petalburg’s Toedscruel also intercepted five passes. I chose Toedscruel; the official winner brought the leading rookie sack total.

Names require care here. Celadon’s Ponyta, who caught 672 yards, is a different player from the Veilstone winner. Vermilion’s fourteen-sack Volbeat is a different player from the Mauville rookie. The club identification is part of the award, not an optional footnote.
Dorrill’s perfect regular season earns the coaching award

Mossdeep went 17–0, scored a league-high 724 points and allowed a league-low 130. Dorrill’s team could give developmental players work late in the season while retaining the conference’s first seed. The Eclipse then reached the final and finished 19–1. The championship defeat will dominate the coach’s own review; it does not change the regular-season achievement being honored.

My vote went to Gardenia after Eterna won eleven games while scoring 214 points. Ellis chose Travis Scarboro for Lavender’s recovery from 4–5 to a division title. Dorian selected Connor McLarren at Mt. Silver. Four very different coaching cases emerged from very different rosters. Dorrill won with the clearest combination of results, scoring and prevention.
Every official All-League selection

The league named 24 players to each team. The table lists the award slot, player and club exactly as a reader needs to distinguish players with shared species names. Mossdeep’s eight first-team places include Marino, BeckhmJr, Ninjaskamara, Gronkaludon, two blockers, Derrat Brooks and Adam Vinathorn. The Psi Corps’ first-team representatives are Lamb, Jack Slampert and Tare.

Mt. Silver placed four players across the two teams and Sunyshore three. Individual recognition also reached well beyond the playoff field: Viridian’s interception leader Sigilyph, Cianwood’s Leafeon and Oreburgh’s Drednaw made the first team. A club’s record tells us what its whole roster accomplished; it does not erase a standout season within that roster.

PSPN’s previously published Pro Bowl selections remain our editorial roster. Twenty official first-team players and nineteen second-team players were on it. The four first-team selections outside that roster were Nacl Stacked, Hearthome’s Swampert, Jack Slampert and Cinnabar’s Doublade. Different conference quotas and role slots produce different teams. We have preserved our original choices so readers can compare them.
How the six PSPN ballots compared

These are the ballots published when the playoffs opened. The match count means agreement with the official winners across six categories. It does not retroactively turn an editorial vote into a prediction, and we have not changed a selection after seeing the result.

Mara and Rowan matched five of six official winners; both missed MVP. Calvin and I matched three, Ellis one and Dorian none. Dorian’s ballot contains several arguments worth debating, particularly the weight given to Lynch’s workload and Matthews’s pressures. It also contains six choices the official awards did not make. Both facts can remain on the page.

Our shared miss was BeckhmJr at the top. Four writers recognized his offensive season and still preferred a quarterback for MVP. The league chose the receiver whose touchdown production separated him from his peers most sharply. That is the result this award edition should lead with.

articles.title: Calvin Rook’s full Season 2 first-round mock draft
articles.dek: Marshadow goes first to Fuchsia, Oreburgh takes the first quarterback, and Calvin makes a fit call for all 32 selections.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: Marshadow is my first pick. Fuchsia needs help getting off the field, and the Gateon State corner brings the rare combination of an 85–99 scouting range, a 4.55 forty and a 48-inch vertical. Snowpoint follows with a safety, Oreburgh bets on its next quarterback, and Fortree finally gets to turn in a card for a blocker.

This is my projection for the first round of the Season 2 draft. The league has yet to number the picks. I’ve used the final Season 1 records, playoff exits and the league’s draft tiebreakers to place all 32 slots. The clubs currently hold their original first-round picks. Free agency and any pick trades can change what teams need and who makes each selection.

The schools, scouting ranges and combine results come from the visible prospect board. The ranges describe what was reported before the draft. They leave room for both better and worse evaluations in camp.
1. Fuchsia Shadows take Marshadow, CB
Gateon State University · Reported range 85–99 · 4.55-second forty · 21 bench reps · 48-inch vertical · 6.10-second three-cone

I would start Fuchsia’s rebuild with the corner who can change the coverage calls. The Shadows went 3–14 and allowed 387 points. Archaludon and Dubwool combined for three regular-season interceptions, and Marshadow gives that room a credible candidate for the hardest outside assignment. Gateon State’s prospect has an 85–99 range, a 4.55 forty and 21 bench repetitions. The 48-inch vertical and 6.10 cone are the numbers I keep coming back to. A corner asked to carry a vertical release still has to reset his feet when the receiver breaks in front of him. Marshadow has a workout that justifies giving him both jobs in camp. Iron Bundle is a serious alternative after Seaking’s retirement, and Fuchsia can spend all spring on the rush. The corner class has a steep drop after this player. I would take Marshadow before anyone else gets a turn.
2. Snowpoint Blizzard take Cryogonal, S
Icirrus University · Reported range 82–99 · 4.61-second forty · 13 bench reps · 39-inch vertical · 6.58-second three-cone

Snowpoint has two young safeties already, which is exactly the room where I would put Cryogonal. Porygon2 and Audino played 526 and 392 regular-season defensive snaps, respectively. Medicham’s retirement takes another 613 snaps and six passes defended out of that picture. Cryogonal has an 82–99 scouting range and a 4.61 forty, the speed I would test first when a safety has to get from the middle to the numbers. The 6.58 cone gives Snowpoint reason to try the Icirrus prospect handling a break underneath, too. I understand the call for Iron Bundle. Twenty team sacks make a pressure pick easy to defend, especially with Sharpedo and Octillery both past 30. I would take the chance to settle a safety job while Audino and Porygon2 are still young enough to grow into complementary ones. Cryogonal gets the first reps deep.
3. Oreburgh Miners take Drampa, QB
Sootopolis State University · Reported range 51–79 · 5.10-second forty · 17 bench reps · 28-inch vertical · 7.28-second three-cone

Oreburgh could bring back the same quarterback plan and still have to answer this question a year from now. Cryogonal finished the season at age 33 and started all 17 games, throwing 15 touchdowns and 13 interceptions. I want the Miners to have a second quarterback ready to compete. The Sootopolis State Drampa is 21. His 51–79 range leads the visible quarterback class, and the 17 bench repetitions stand out in that room. The 5.10 forty and 7.28 cone would make me build his first evaluation from the pocket. Let him show that he can work through a second answer while Drednaw and the defense give him time to learn. Dracozolt would make a stronger case on a straight athletic board, but Oreburgh already has an 11.5-sack end in Drednaw. Pick three is early for a quarterback with this wide a range. I would make the investment anyway.
4. Fortree Skyhawks take Lapras, OL
Agate State University · Reported range 77–99 · 4.95-second forty · 17 bench reps · 33-inch vertical · 6.91-second three-cone

I kept a Fortree folder through a lot of Sundays this season. Sixty-two team sacks allowed put Lapras on the first page. Rabsca took 59 in sixteen starts, and the line’s oldest regular was 32-year-old Camerupt. There is room to improve the protection while younger blockers like Turtonator establish themselves. The Agate State lineman has a 77–99 range, a 4.95 forty and a 6.91 cone. That is enough movement for me to start his camp evaluation at tackle and see how consistently he can redirect against a second move. Dracozolt has a strong case for a defense that allowed 413 points, made 17 sacks and lost Mawile to retirement. Lapras gets my vote because I want Fortree to find out what Rabsca and those young receivers can do with a cleaner first read. Give the offense a fair test.
5. Viridian Titans take Iron Bundle, OLB
Shalour Military Academy · Reported range 69–97 · 4.53-second forty · 17 bench reps · 47-inch vertical · 5.96-second three-cone

Viridian lost outside linebacker Volbeat and inside linebacker Wigglytuff to retirement. Volbeat made eight of the Titans’ 22 regular-season sacks and supplied 30 pressures. At five, I would take the outside player who makes me ask a protection coach how much help he wants to send. Iron Bundle’s 4.53 forty, 47-inch vertical and 5.96 cone all back up that question, and the 69–97 range is strong enough to give it some weight. Shalour’s prospect also put up 17 bench reps. I would start with the passing-down job and add space responsibilities when the staff has seen him read the route combination. Agate State’s Throh is available and could address the other retirement immediately. Viridian has a better chance of finding an inside option elsewhere on this board. I would make the call for Iron Bundle here.
6. Azalea Swarm take Seviper, WR
University of Celadon · Reported range 62–90 · 4.95-second forty · 19 bench reps · 34-inch vertical · 6.87-second three-cone

Azalea scored 182 points, and its two most established listed receivers are Pyroar and Vivillon, ages 32 and 30. Their combined 1,226 regular-season receiving yards deserve respect. I would use the sixth pick to build the next outside partnership while both can still take reps with the newcomer. The University of Celadon’s Seviper has a 62–90 range and 19 bench repetitions, a strength result worth following into contested-release work. The 4.95 forty leaves me more interested in how he gets to the catch point on an in-breaker than in how often he runs past everybody. Drampa threw 11 touchdowns this season, so I want the staff to give him a receiver he can test in traffic. Dhelmise presents a better range at tight end. My jersey would have Seviper’s name on it because two outside succession decisions are already on Azalea’s desk.
7. Mahogany Frost take Dhelmise, TE
University of Santalune · Reported range 80–99 · 5.06-second forty · 28 bench reps · 30-inch vertical · 7.24-second three-cone

Porygon-Z threw 21 touchdowns against eight interceptions, and Mahogany’s 5–11–1 finish came with a points deficit of just 12. Give that quarterback a larger part of the middle of the field. The Frost lost Gastrodon to retirement after 283 receiving yards and two touchdowns from a fullback listing. Their two most-used listed tight ends, Granbull and Lileep, combined for 124 receiving yards. Dhelmise comes out of Santalune with an 80–99 range and 28 bench repetitions. I would ask him to work the short middle and make the first block on the edge before I send him down the seam. The 5.06 forty and 7.24 cone describe a strength-led workout. Blackthorn’s Miltank would be a good backfield investment here, too. With a receiver or blocker’s job available from the same alignment, I’d put Dhelmise in the huddle.
8. Veilstone Fists take Qwilfish, OLB
Mid-Galar State University · Reported range 67–95 · 4.81-second forty · 17 bench reps · 41-inch vertical · 6.42-second three-cone

Veilstone can pair Octillery with another rusher and let both keep offensive tackles busy. Octillery made ten regular-season sacks and Scizor supplied 49 pressures. Sandslash has retired after 17 starts, 3.5 sacks and 23 pressures, so Qwilfish has a real path to playing time. Mid-Galar State’s outside linebacker pairs a 67–95 range with a 4.81 forty and 6.42 cone. When the first step wins him half a man, I want to find out whether that change of direction lets him finish the rush or come back inside. The workouts make the idea worth testing. Lavaridge’s Klefki is a defensible safety alternative with Ampharos at 30, and the offense has questions after 185 points. An outside linebacker with these results and an open role is the cleanest bet on this part of the board. I expect the Fists to make it.
9. Pewter Rockers take Furfrou, CB
Po State University · Reported range 60–88 · 4.80-second forty · 15 bench reps · 41-inch vertical · 6.37-second three-cone

Froslass retired after 12 starts, four interceptions and 13 passes defended. Pewter already found 37 sacks last season, so the most direct way to protect that defense is to draft a corner who can capitalize on rushed throws. Po State’s Furfrou has a 60–88 range, a 41-inch vertical and a 6.37 cone. The jump gives me something to watch at the boundary, and the cone gives me a reason to put him in an off-coverage drill on the first day. Start him in a competition with Tentacool beside Golbat, who defended 11 passes. Fortree’s Girafarig is the alternative I would take seriously after Wyrdeer’s 13 touchdowns and 15 picks. At nine I give the roster and the workout a vote together. A recorded retirement has opened a real job, and Furfrou is my top corner after Marshadow.
10. Celadon Bloom take Miltank, HB
University of Blackthorn · Reported range 65–93 · 4.72-second forty · 22 bench reps · 40-inch vertical · 6.58-second three-cone

Celadon’s running back need looks different when you follow the carries. Seaking was listed at outside linebacker, yet he rushed for 645 yards and three touchdowns before retiring. Diggersby supplied 239 yards and is 29. If I draft Miltank here, the first assignment is to find out whether she can take the ordinary early-down work that nobody in this backfield has secured for the next season. The Blackthorn prospect has a 65–93 range, 22 bench reps, a 4.72 forty and a 40-inch vertical. I want to see that burst through the first crease with a defender square to the line. Levincia’s Comfey would address two 31-year-old safeties, and there is a case for choosing the secondary with this pick. I would give a team that scored 207 points a dependable source of touches to build around first.
11. Pastoria Waves take Comfey, S
University of Levincia · Reported range 77–99 · 4.67-second forty · 12 bench reps · 40-inch vertical · 6.31-second three-cone

Pastoria finished 6–11 and lost a safety who played 746 regular-season defensive snaps. Azumarill’s retirement gives the Waves a decision about how often they want to leave a safety with space behind him. Comfey’s 77–99 range has the class’s top group written all over it. The University of Levincia prospect ran a 4.67 forty and a 6.31 cone, the combination I want at the top of routes that can break in either direction. Togekiss is 26 and already has a year’s worth of work to compare. Let him and Comfey run alternating deep and underneath assignments before settling the pairing. I would consider Dracozolt if I wanted to add another end, but Banette and Arctibax already combined for 18.5 sacks at outside linebacker. I’d put the premium pick into the newly open back-end work and let that rush stay aggressive.
12. Sootopolis Surge take Sigilyph, S
Sonia University · Reported range 77–99 · 4.84-second forty · 10 bench reps · 42-inch vertical · 6.43-second three-cone

Sootopolis needs to account for a full season of Pachirisu’s work. The retired safety started 17 games, played 953 defensive snaps and logged 90 tackles, three interceptions and 12 passes defended. Sonia University’s Sigilyph shows a 77–99 range and a 42-inch vertical. Put him in a drill where the ball arrives high and a receiver can force him to take an indirect route to it. The 6.43 cone is good enough to give me ideas about how he might move between a high assignment and a driving break. Petalburg’s Sigilyph ran a quicker forty and is a legitimate alternative, with a 70–98 range. I prefer the 21-year-old Sonia prospect’s range and jump for the breadth of work the Surge need to replace. Rebuilding the rush would be fair after 23 sacks. This available safety is worth taking first.
13. Cerulean Tide take Dracozolt, DE
Turffield State University · Reported range 64–92 · 4.82-second forty · 19 bench reps · 33-inch vertical · 6.85-second three-cone

Cerulean made 17 sacks. Chesnaught was responsible for eight, and he and Golurk combined for 71 pressures. The Tide have a starting point for a credible rush, and I want them to add an end with the quickness to turn those snaps into fewer clean escapes. Turffield State’s Dracozolt comes with a 64–92 range, 19 bench reps and a 4.82 forty. I would watch him run the corner and then give him a tackle who sets wide enough to force a decision back inside. The 6.85 cone supports that test. Eiscue has the stronger range on the offensive line, and Cerulean has 31 sacks allowed and a 33-year-old Marowak to consider there. I would take Dracozolt because the top end of this class still offers a useful partnership with Chesnaught. The other end prospects ask for more projection.
14. Lavaridge Inferno take Eiscue, OL
Paniola State University · Reported range 71–99 · 4.95-second forty · 19 bench reps · 31-inch vertical · 6.96-second three-cone

Delphox threw 22 touchdowns and took 40 sacks. Lavaridge can keep the workable part of that offense and give its quarterback a better chance on the slower-developing throws. There is a 31-year-old Eiscue in the Inferno’s line already. The new one comes from Paniola State, is 21 and brings a 71–99 range. A 4.95 forty and 19 bench repetitions tell me to start the evaluation with both strength and movement assignments on the same practice script. I want to see him establish contact on one snap and get to a second defender on the next. Sunyshore’s Klawf ran faster and posted more bench reps, which makes him an attractive alternative. I prefer Eiscue’s higher scouting range and extra developmental time for a line that should have room to fit the best five together. That is my pick for the Inferno.
15. Cianwood Crushers take Arctozolt, TE
Lavender Forest University · Reported range 67–95 · 4.87-second forty · 20 bench reps · 31-inch vertical · 7.18-second three-cone

Cianwood allowed 240 points and finished 8–9. I would pay for more ways to turn its 223 points into leads. Bibarel rushed for 1,087 yards, and the listed tight end with the most regular-season starts, 30-year-old Arctovish, put up 185 receiving yards. Arctozolt’s 67–95 range and 20 bench repetitions give Lavender Forest’s prospect a good case to earn blocking work next to the line. The 4.87 forty gives the passing game a reason to move him away from it and see whether a linebacker can carry him. Cianwood gave up 13 sacks, so there is room here to buy a target instead of another protector. Sycamore’s Gastly offers a more obvious outside receiving bet. I would choose Arctozolt because the best part of this offense can stay on the field while the staff tests that extra route.
16. Canalave Bulwark take Gastly, WR
Sycamore University · Reported range 57–85 · 4.82-second forty · 4 bench reps · 41-inch vertical · 6.53-second three-cone

Canalave finished 8–9 while scoring 183 points. Neither of its two most-used listed wide receivers reached 300 receiving yards, and Delcatty and Manectric combined for two scores. Slowking completed a season with nine touchdown passes and five interceptions. I would give the Bulwark a receiver who can make the field a little larger before I decide what their quarterback can be. Sycamore’s Gastly has a 57–85 range, 41-inch vertical and 6.53 cone. I want to see him win early against a corner who can make him restart his route. Four bench reps give the staff a good reason to test that release in pads. Hulbury’s Delibird has almost the same range and more bench reps. The quicker forty and cone make Gastly my pick. He can begin with a package that lets him work with space off the line.
17. Violet Falcons take Girafarig, QB
University of Fortree · Reported range 43–71 · 4.82-second forty · 14 bench reps · 37-inch vertical · 6.51-second three-cone

Iron Jugulis threw for 3,371 yards and started all 17 games. The 21 interceptions put an alternate plan on Violet’s agenda, and Jugulis is 30. Fortree’s Girafarig offers a 43–71 range, a 4.82 forty and a 6.51 cone. I would use movement to give him some early answers, then ask him to win the job with the throws he can make from a set pocket. The testing gives me more reason to get him into a camp than to hand him a Week 1 job. Solaceon’s Heatmor would add help for a defense that conceded 314 points and recorded 25 sacks. I like that fit if Violet has already settled its future quarterback in another way. On the roster in front of me, I would get the prospect working behind Jugulis and let the staff take its time.
18. Mauville Dynamos take Heatmor, DE
Solaceon University · Reported range 53–81 · 4.98-second forty · 19 bench reps · 37-inch vertical · 6.80-second three-cone

Mauville got 13 sacks from rookie outside linebacker Volbeat. It also got nine combined from Drednaw and Gyarados, both 32 at season’s end. The Dynamos can set up the next end rotation while there is still something to learn from the old one. Solaceon’s Heatmor brings a 53–81 range, with 19 bench repetitions and a 6.80 cone. Put him at end in a practice period with an actual tackle in front of him, then see if he can re-enter the rush after initial contact. Granbull has a stronger range at tackle, but Mudsdale and Torterra are 24 and 26 and each produced two regular-season sacks from the interior group. Mauville has enough to work with there. I would give Volbeat a young end whose progress can be judged on the same pass-rush snaps, with a role that still makes sense next year.
19. Hearthome Haunts take Throh, ILB
Agate State University · Reported range 71–99 · 5.05-second forty · 18 bench reps · 31-inch vertical · 7.02-second three-cone

The Haunts made the playoffs at 8–8–1. Their inside group is led by a 33-year-old Conkeldurr who made 48 tackles and seven tackles for loss. Agate State’s Throh is my first inside linebacker, with a 71–99 range and 18 bench repetitions. I want him in the traffic Conkeldurr has been handling. The 5.05 forty and 7.02 cone give me a workout I can use to talk about fitting a run on time, with the tape work still to come. Mahogany’s Throh is younger and logged 20 reps, and he makes sense if Hearthome puts the later development curve first. The six-point difference in both range endpoints gives Agate the edge for this team. Start the prospect on work between the tackles. Hearthome can evaluate whether he earns more coverage responsibility from there.
20. Olivine Ironclads take Granbull, DT
University of Pyrite · Reported range 65–93 · 5.01-second forty · 15 bench reps · 32-inch vertical · 6.97-second three-cone

Olivine has an outside rusher in Darmanitan, who supplied 12 of its 29 regular-season sacks and 51 pressures. Cetitan played 368 defensive snaps and recorded half a sack, and young nose tackle Torterra gives the front a separate role to develop. Pyrite’s Granbull would give me a reason to try more interior rush snaps and make a quarterback feel the space Darmanitan takes away outside. The 65–93 range is the best at listed defensive tackle. The 5.01 forty and 15 bench reps are useful starting points for testing a first step and what happens when the guard meets it. I would keep Cascarrafa’s Trubbish in the conversation with Veluza and Bibarel both 30. The larger visible range at a harder-to-fill defensive job gets my vote. Granbull can fight for a passing-down role with a well-defined purpose in his first camp.
21. Rustboro Stone take Mawile, OLB
University of Cyllage · Reported range 62–90 · 4.98-second forty · 14 bench reps · 35-inch vertical · 6.89-second three-cone

Rustboro scored 336 points and allowed 342 behind a defense that recorded 17 sacks. GET HIM! supplied 36 pressures and four sacks at 31. I want another front-seven player who can help the Stone make a third-and-long count. Cyllage’s Mawile is 21 with a 62–90 range, a 4.98 forty and a 6.89 cone. Both times beat Porto Marinada’s Sableye, who shares the range and 14 bench reps. That is a small enough difference to keep Sableye in the room and a consistent enough one to make Mawile my choice. Put him on selected rush snaps with the older end and let him learn what winning the first step buys. Rustboro lost Watchog from the backfield, too, but Philly Gabite already ran for 870 yards and 11 touchdowns. My first-round pick gives Rustboro a young outside linebacker to go with that offense.
22. Vermilion Volts take Delibird, WR
University of Hulbury · Reported range 56–84 · 4.92-second forty · 8 bench reps · 41-inch vertical · 6.62-second three-cone

Vermilion won ten games with 210 points. Victreebel’s retirement removes 645 receiving yards and five touchdowns, and Galvantula put up 414 yards and two scores. I would take a listed receiver who can start repaying some of those targets. Hulbury’s Delibird has a 56–84 range and a 41-inch vertical, which puts the contested catch on my practice list. A 4.92 forty gives me more interest in the timing of a break than in sending him downfield all afternoon. Central Sinnoh’s Meowth presents the more explosive speed workout, with a 4.71 forty and 6.27 cone. I can see the argument for building the play menu around that option. Vermilion needs a receiver who can win a larger share of ordinary downs as well. I would start with Delibird’s stronger reported range and give him an early chance alongside Galvantula.
23. Eterna Thorns take Torkoal, OL
University of Cinnabar · Reported range 68–96 · 5.21-second forty · 18 bench reps · 30-inch vertical · 7.24-second three-cone

Eterna allowed only 184 points and reached the playoffs, but its offense gave up 42 sacks. Slowking and Tatsugiri took 40 of those between them. The Thorns can help both quarterbacks by clearing the first read on the line of scrimmage. Torkoal’s 68–96 range is strong at this point, and the University of Cinnabar prospect recorded 18 bench repetitions. His 5.21 forty and 7.24 cone make me want an initial look inside, where I can see how much space he holds when the rush comes directly through him. I would see whether he can challenge for a role alongside the younger Metang, Naclstack and Audino as the group settles. Icirrus’s Woobat is an option for a receiving corps short on production. I’d give the current passers a chance to stay upright before using this pick on their next target.
24. Cinnabar Blaze take Carnivine, DE
University of Agate · Reported range 52–80 · 5.03-second forty · 16 bench reps · 32-inch vertical · 6.96-second three-cone

Cinnabar’s offense scored 366 points behind Gholdengo’s 30 touchdown passes, and its secondary has young production from Tatsugiri and cornerback Thievul. Defensive end is where I want another option. Scizor generated 41 regular-season pressures and came away with one sack. University of Agate’s Carnivine has a 52–80 range, a 5.03 forty and a 6.96 cone. I would use him in the rotation opposite Scizor and see if the two can make the escape route smaller together. Vermilion Metropolitan’s Cranidos matches the range and finished three more bench reps. Choose him if the job calls for greater emphasis on setting the edge. I am willing to bet on Agate’s slightly quicker forty for this first job, with the run-defense work still to prove. The Blaze can look for that specialist while its offense keeps pressuring opponents on the scoreboard.
25. Dewford Breakers take Castform, OLB
University of Medali · Reported range 56–84 · 4.91-second forty · 13 bench reps · 38-inch vertical · 6.70-second three-cone

Dewford’s retiring outside linebackers make this choice plain. Ambipom and Kricketune combined for eight of the Breakers’ 23 sacks, and the 11–6 team needs to replace two separate sets of snaps. Medali’s Castform has a 56–84 range with a 4.91 forty, 38-inch vertical and 6.70 cone. His movement results make me want to try a job where the call can change from rushing to matching a back without changing the player. Porto Marinada’s Sableye carries a higher range and could be the pick if Dewford is shopping for the most convincing broad projection. The coaching staff still has Watchog, who made five sacks, and 23-year-old Unfezant to build around. I would take Castform for a role that can coexist with either and let them prove where the steady rush comes from. Both retirees’ work deserves more than one answer.
26. Lavender Wails take Throh, ILB
University of Mahogany · Reported range 65–93 · 5.07-second forty · 20 bench reps · 31-inch vertical · 7.04-second three-cone

Lavender must replace two starting linebackers after the retirements of EARTHQUAKE!!! and Mr. Joe. Mr. Joe started all 17 games and accounted for 744 regular-season defensive snaps, while EARTHQUAKE!!! logged another 783. A 21-year-old inside linebacker I already like is available. The University of Mahogany’s Throh tested at 20 bench repetitions with a 65–93 range. Ask him to hold his ground when the ball comes inside, then ask him to move off that spot in coverage. The 7.04 cone tells me to make the second question a priority. Lilycove’s Bouffalant matched the bench mark and ran a quicker forty. I prefer the Mahogany prospect’s slightly higher range, with a clear place to begin the evaluation. Lavender needs new answers outside, too. I would secure the interior option here and make the other assignment a distinct search.
27. Petalburg Pride take Trubbish, TE
University of Cascarrafa · Reported range 56–84 · 4.91-second forty · 15 bench reps · 36-inch vertical · 6.77-second three-cone

Petalburg put up 286 points in a 12–5 season. Iron Valiant threw 24 touchdowns, and 31-year-old Seviper supplied 544 receiving yards and four scores from tight end. Trubbish gives the Pride a chance to test the next player for that job while Seviper still carries the familiar assignments. Cascarrafa’s prospect is 21, with a 56–84 range, 4.91 forty, 36-inch vertical and 6.77 cone. I want to see him change direction into a short window and catch away from his body before I ask him to take an entire formation’s blocking work. Icirrus’s Woobat brings a similar movement argument for the outside receivers. The larger range and a more direct succession plan put Trubbish ahead for me. If he can make himself useful in the short game early, the Pride can build the rest of the role in camp.
28. Blackthorn Dragons take Klawf, OL
University of Sunyshore · Reported range 65–93 · 4.86-second forty · 21 bench reps · 33-inch vertical · 6.83-second three-cone

Blackthorn’s Hatterene threw for 4,532 yards and 38 touchdowns. He also took 50 sacks. The Dragons had four regular linemen aged 30 or older at season’s end, including Lickilickelce, Clodsire, Bellibolt and Simeon Ice. Klawf gives them a candidate to bring into that group before several jobs open at once. The University of Sunyshore lineman recorded 21 bench repetitions, a 4.86 forty and a 6.83 cone along with a 65–93 range. I would start his work with a protection assignment that forces him to move laterally and then anchor on contact. Mauville’s Shuckle is younger and edges the range by one point, which is an attractive succession case in itself. I think Blackthorn can make immediate use of Klawf’s movement profile. The speed of that offense already shows up with the ball out, and I want him helping give Hatterene the full count to get there.
29. Sunyshore Starseekers take Sigilyph, S
Petalburg University · Reported range 70–98 · 4.73-second forty · 12 bench reps · 41-inch vertical · 6.44-second three-cone

Sunyshore lost @mped UP after 17 starts and 790 regular-season defensive snaps. It also allowed four passing touchdowns in the conference championship. My pick is Petalburg’s Sigilyph, a safety with a 70–98 range, a 4.73 forty and a 6.44 cone. I would have Sunyshore work him through the two checks a new deep player will have to make with Pat Serptain and Serp Gardener. Serptain defended 18 passes, and Gardener intercepted three, so a prospect can join a secondary that has established players to work with. University of Lavaridge’s Klefki offers 15 bench reps and a 62–90 range, which would appeal for a more contact-heavy role. I prefer this Sigilyph for reach and recovery on the back end. He gets the first audition for some of the snaps that left in retirement.
30. Mt. Silver Reds take Sableye, OLB
Porto Marinada Coastal University · Reported range 62–90 · 5.07-second forty · 14 bench reps · 33-inch vertical · 6.96-second three-cone

Blayz Matthews accounted for 17.5 of the Reds’ 27 regular-season sacks and collected 70 pressures. Mt. Silver also lost outside linebacker depth when Medicham retired. I would give its most productive rusher another outside linebacker who can earn a useful snap when the offense knows it has to throw. Porto Marinada’s Sableye has a 62–90 range, 14 bench repetitions and a 5.07 forty. The 6.96 cone asks for a camp test with a tackle who can stay square. Hau’oli State’s Grookey ran quicker in both movement drills and would make sense if change of direction drives the role. The stronger range and bench result move Sableye ahead on my board. Put him in the rotation and see if he can make protections honor the other side before Matthews has already finished the play.
31. Mossdeep Eclipse take Shuckle, OL
University of Mauville · Reported range 66–94 · 5.19-second forty · 16 bench reps · 28-inch vertical · 7.27-second three-cone

Mossdeep had two 33-year-old linemen start every regular-season game. Crust Alstott and Bastony Boseli were part of a group that gave up just 27 sacks, which buys the Eclipse a chance to work in a successor with some patience. The University of Mauville’s Shuckle is 21 with a 66–94 range. His 5.19 forty and 7.27 cone give me a stronger reason to test him inside than to hand him the tackle assignment. The scouting bounds give that experiment room to pay off. Lavaridge’s Klefki would address the retirement of Luvrelle Revis and is my defensive alternative. Mossdeep has enough veterans up front to show a young blocker how a good protection should look. I would spend this pick on preserving the conditions Dram Marino had while he threw 56 regular-season touchdown passes, then find a separate answer at safety.
32. Saffron Psi Corps take Misdreavus, CB
Central Unova University · Reported range 57–85 · 4.74-second forty · 10 bench reps · 42-inch vertical · 6.41-second three-cone

Saffron enters the offseason with wide receiver Jolt Train Ln and safety Fliff Farris atop its two corner spots. Train defended 20 passes and Farris defended 15 during the regular season. Those players earned their work. A rookie corner would give the champions more choices about where they can use them. Central Unova’s Misdreavus brings a 57–85 range, a 4.74 forty and a 42-inch vertical. Ten bench repetitions make me want to see him handle contact, so I would begin with off-coverage work and build the camp competition from there. North Orre’s Tropius is an appealing line option with a 63–91 range. I would take the corner while this defense can give him snaps behind a rush that made 78 sacks in 17 regular-season games. He would get a manageable start with a clear route to more.

articles.title: Nineteen wins, one loss and an offseason Mossdeep will feel
articles.dek: The Eclipse’s final brings an MVP injury, two squandered scoring opportunities and a painful distinction between the season they built and the championship they wanted.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Michael Dorrill has a Coach of the Year award and a game he will want to discuss first. This is entirely consistent with the man who spent a perfect regular season finding the next assignment to correct. It is also a particularly cruel way to meet him at the end of it. Mossdeep won nineteen games, lost the twentieth by seven points, and had its league MVP leave in the first quarter of the only defeat.

I picked the Eclipse to win the Indigo Bowl. I watched the reasons for that prediction remain visible even as the game moved away from them. Dram Marino could still complete a difficult third-down pass. Ninjaskamara could still turn a short throw into useful ground. The defense could still produce the stop that gave the offense one more opportunity. Those capacities brought Mossdeep back within an onside kick of another possession. Saffron recovered it, and capacities became something to discuss during the offseason.

There is no attractive way to arrange that sentence for the people who lost. A 19–1 record is an extraordinary season to have and a difficult season to finish describing when the single loss is the final. The players can understand both facts without being asked to appreciate the first one on command.
BeckhmJr’s season ends in two very different reports

Accel BeckhmJr is the official Most Valuable Player and Offensive Player of the Year. He is also listed with a nineteen-week injury from the Indigo Bowl. His final-game receiving line contains one catch for ten yards. The award recognizes a regular season of exceptional production; the box score records how little of the championship he could play.

The duration on the injury report deserves attention without becoming a diagnosis or a guessed return date. The league has entered its offseason, and the next availability update will matter. Nobody can turn the current counter into a confident account of next season’s missed games simply by reading it aloud. What Mossdeep already knows is the absence it had to manage in the final.

Brooks caught five passes for ninety-four yards. That is Derrat Brooks, the linebacker who also appears on the official first All-League team at outside linebacker. He was Marino’s most productive receiver in the final. Ninjulio Jones added eighty-four yards; Ninjaskamara added seventy-two. The receiving work tells you something about the disruption without requiring anyone to pretend that a replacement assignment recreates BeckhmJr.

“You catch the one he throws you,” Brooks said. “Then you come back and do the next job. There wasn’t time to decide whether it was an unusual afternoon.” It is the sort of practical answer Brooks gives when the question is trying to make him sound more surprised than he feels.

I would resist making his production a neat consolation story. He helped. Mossdeep still lost. The useful offseason discussion is about how the offense kept finding completions after losing its best receiver, and how much more difficult the rest of its work became.
The opportunities that will survive every review

Mossdeep’s first-half turnovers will be easy to find on film. Marino’s opening possession ended with Fliff Farris intercepting a deep pass to the right. A later drive ended with Ninjaskamara fumbling a completed pass and Pach Tatum recovering. The Eclipse reached halftime with no points, having given away two possessions that offered a chance to score.

The second loss of possession was followed by Saffron’s ninety-six-yard field-goal drive. That made the sequence especially expensive. Mossdeep had been moving toward a score of its own; Saffron instead extended its lead to 10–0. You can acknowledge the uncertainty of what an uninterrupted drive might have produced and still understand why that exchange hurts.

“We don’t need to invent a different game,” Dorrill said. “We need to look at the plays we had. Protect the football. Finish the possession. Cover the next down. Those were our responsibilities before the injury, and they were our responsibilities after it.”

His team scored on three of its four second-half possessions: a Diggs touchdown, a Vinathorn field goal and, after a turnover on downs and a defensive stand, the late Ninjaskamara touchdown. The sequence included enough resistance to keep the score close, and enough Saffron answers to keep the Eclipse behind. Every improvement arrived with another task attached.

The first third-quarter touchdown narrowed the margin to three. Saffron answered with Lamb’s thirty-seven-yard touchdown catch. Vinathorn’s fourth-quarter field goal cut it to seven. Saffron answered with Pawmo’s touchdown catch. Marino’s last drive cut it back to seven with seventeen seconds left after the extra point. There was finally no time for a conventional defensive answer.
The record still belongs to these players

Mossdeep scored 724 points and allowed 130 in seventeen regular-season wins. Its three playoff games brought the full-season totals to 818 scored and 188 allowed. The Eclipse won their conference, then lost the championship to a club they had beaten 20–17 during the regular season. Saffron found a way to make the second meeting different. Both games belong in the account.

The official awards also belong there. Marino is first-team All-League at quarterback, Ninjaskamara at running back, BeckhmJr at receiver and Gronkaludon at tight end. Crust Alstott and Tyran Armstead made the first team on the offensive line, Brooks at outside linebacker and Adam Vinathorn at kicker. Ninjulio, Bastony Boseli and Ronnie Watt earned second-team places. Eleven selections are a substantial record of the work that got Mossdeep to the final.

Those honors describe a roster that repeatedly played excellent football. They do not settle every argument about the last game. Dorrill can take pride in the players and demand an exact account of the two turnovers. Marino can have earned his first-team place and want the intercepted throw back. BeckhmJr can be the league’s MVP and still have almost no opportunity to influence its last afternoon.

I distrust the speed with which a championship defeat can make people talk about an entire season as if it were a clerical error. Nineteen wins required work. So did Saffron’s four playoff wins. The final gave the latter team the trophy; it did not remove the former team’s games from the schedule.
The next roster begins with an actual departure

Luvrelle Revis has retired. The thirty-year-old safety’s departure is confirmed in the offseason records, making the first change to Mossdeep’s next roster more concrete than any mock-draft speculation. His name appears throughout the final’s defensive play log. The team will now have to account for that job without him.

Gyarls Woodson’s fourth-down stop of Skattebo supplied Mossdeep’s final possession. It is a useful place to begin discussing the younger players: an actual assignment, an actual stop, and a chance earned. D’Brickabone, Gyarls and several other younger players also finished the update a level higher. Development will continue to matter when the next set of available players arrives, but the offseason has only reached the coaching-staff stage. There is still a draft and a series of roster decisions ahead.
“We’ll review it properly,” Marino said. “There were plays we made and plays we didn’t make. The guys who came into different jobs gave us chances. I want to get those chances finished.”
The last of them ended at the Mossdeep forty-nine, where Saffron recovered the onside kick. Dorrill will have nineteen wins in the season file and that final recovery at the end of the film.

articles.title: Saffron made the favorite answer until the clock ran out
articles.dek: Trent Scarboro’s champions converted the difficult downs, protected the ball and answered every Mossdeep score. Their four-win playoff run deserves the full account.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Trent Scarboro, you have my attention. You had it when Saffron knocked out Mt. Silver, which remains a sentence I would prefer somebody else to read. You kept it when the Psi Corps took a ten-point halftime lead over Mossdeep. And you earned the final word when Crustle recovered the onside kick and Archam Manning knelt to finish the Indigo Bowl.

Saffron is the champion. Four playoff games, four wins, 142 points scored and 63 allowed. The Psi Corps beat Olivine, Lavender, Mt. Silver and Mossdeep. Every opponent on that list had earned a playoff place. The last one arrived unbeaten. Scarboro’s team sent all four into the offseason.

I picked Saffron 27–24 in the final. It won 24–17. That gave me the correct winner and the closest of our five final-week score predictions, which I intend to mention with a frequency my colleagues will find professionally unnecessary. It does not repair my original bracket, in which I chose Mt. Silver. The champions beat the club I thought would win and then beat the club most of the room thought would win. They have supplied a thorough answer.
The fourth downs belonged to Saffron’s receivers

The final’s first touchdown drive required Saffron to survive a sack and convert fourth-and-two. HeeDee Lamb caught the pass for ten yards. The drive that restored a ten-point lead in the third quarter also required Saffron to survive a sack and convert fourth-and-two. Gengar Pickens caught that one for nine. If you want a practical description of a championship offense, start with the receivers who let it keep playing.

Manning was 21-of-29 for 337 yards, two touchdowns and no interception. He completed every one of his six throws to Pickens for eighty-four yards. Lamb caught seven for 153 and the third-quarter touchdown. Mothel Irving caught four for sixty-five. The distribution mattered because Mossdeep could win an individual down and still face a different receiver on the next one.

Lamb’s thirty-seven-yard touchdown will receive the large photograph. Good. It should. His earlier twenty-five-yard catch on third-and-eight and ten-yard catch on fourth-and-two deserve room in the same conversation. A spectacular finish has more value when your receiver has already helped prevent the possession from ending.

“We had to keep earning it,” Pickens said. “I expected the ball when we needed a first down. That’s why I run the route.” There is a pleasing absence of apology in that answer. Saffron had already watched the defense put its quarterback behind schedule. Pickens treated the next target as a job to complete.
Skattebo’s smaller rushing total still had value

My preview put Dam Skattebo at the center of Saffron’s plan. He finished with fifty rushing yards on fifteen carries, a two-yard touchdown, and twenty-eight receiving yards on three catches. That is a different statistical shape from the conference championship. It also includes several of the gains that let Saffron control its final touchdown drive.

Joey Sporeter sacked Manning to open that possession. Skattebo immediately ran for twelve yards on second-and-fourteen. Pickens converted the remaining two. Skattebo then caught passes for seventeen and five yards, helping move the Psi Corps toward the scoring chance Pawmo finished. The possession used a back who could contribute after the run call had already done its work.

I will happily defend the preview’s argument with those plays. I will also acknowledge that Lamb and Manning supplied the final’s most decisive offensive production. A useful prediction can identify part of the solution without becoming a claim that every subsequent yard was secretly its idea. My colleagues may print that sentence and put it near my desk.

Pawmo’s seven-yard touchdown catch made it 23–10, and Octillery’s extra point extended the lead to fourteen. The same receiver had helped the late first-half field-goal drive with a sixteen-yard run. Saffron found contributions from its principal stars and from the player who received its last touchdown pass. The championship offense gave Manning several reliable options when Mossdeep concentrated on the leading targets.
Tare gave the defense four separate interventions

NeMarcus Tare is the official Defensive Player of the Year, and he finished the final with four sacks. He sacked Dram Marino on Mossdeep’s first offensive snap. He got him again on a second-quarter possession, again during the long third-quarter touchdown drive, and again when Mossdeep was trying to answer the touchdown that made it 24–10.

The last of those sacks pushed the Eclipse toward third-and-seventeen. Their fourth-down completion gained fourteen. Saffron took possession. You do not need to pretend every sack ended a drive to see the importance of that one. It changed the distance the offense had to recover at a point when the clock and score were already making the assignment difficult.

Saffron’s defense also took the football twice. Fliff Farris intercepted Marino’s deep-right pass during the opening Mossdeep drive, and Pach Tatum recovered Ninjaskamara’s second-quarter fumble. The offense produced a touchdown after the interception and a field goal after the fumble. Mossdeep’s defense had to return to work; Saffron’s offense received the chance to extend its stay.

I am not going to write Accel BeckhmJr out of this game’s explanation. The MVP went out in the first quarter after one catch. Mossdeep had to reorganize its receiving work, and the final was poorer for having so little of him in it. Saffron still had to execute the possessions it was given. The champions did that often enough to remain in front every time the Eclipse scored.
The season contained a correction

Mossdeep beat Saffron 20–17 in Week 10. Mt. Silver beat Saffron in Week 15. The Psi Corps met both opponents again during this postseason and won both rematches. That is a concrete account of improvement: the same clubs, a different outcome, and recorded plays explaining how the winning possessions continued.

Scarboro has spent the season asking his players to keep believing in the next assignment. It would be easy to turn his championship speech into a general statement about belief. The final provides more interesting material. Lamb on fourth-and-two. Pickens on fourth-and-two. Skattebo answering a sack with twelve yards. Tare making a late passing down harder. Crustle securing the onside kick.

“Those guys know what they gave each other,” Scarboro said. “Sometimes it’s the touchdown. Sometimes it’s catching the ball that lets somebody else score later. They stayed with each other through all of it.”

Saffron finished 14–3 in the regular season and 18–3 overall. It did not receive the conference’s first-round bye. It took the longer route, then beat the two top seeds in successive weeks. My original championship pick went home in the conference final. My final-week pick recovered the onside kick and won the trophy.

articles.dek: The staff reopens its saved picks, brackets and award ballots after 221 graded games.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I had every game of the opening playoff bracket right until the one Mossdeep needed most. Twelve winners, the correct championship pairing and a 34–27 Eclipse pick that Saffron turned into a 24–17 defeat. I can explain why I liked Mossdeep. I cannot put that explanation in the win column.

This is the end-of-season review of PSPN’s forecasts. The weekly ledger begins with Week 5 and contains 208 regular-season games plus thirteen playoff games. We graded those 221 games using the picks we actually published. Tessa Wren finished first at 148–72–1. Rowan Vale was the only writer who picked Saffron to win the championship before the playoffs began. Ellis Quill collected the most closest-score bonuses. Those are separate accomplishments, and combining them into one convenient victory would be an excellent way for all five of us to claim first place.
Tessa wins the weekly picks

Tessa finished seven correct selections ahead of me and eleven ahead of Rowan. The advantage survived the entire postseason: she correctly selected ten of thirteen playoff winners, including the two conference champions. Her final pick was Mossdeep 31–26, so she joined me in losing the last selection. A season table can accommodate that mistake. She had already built the best record over the largest set of games we graded.

Her exact Mauville 23–17 win over Fortree in Week 12 was one of three perfect score calls in the ledger. Ellis and I both had Cinnabar 27–10 over Pewter in Week 6. Three exact calls across 221 games should discourage anyone from pretending the last digit of a forecast arrives with much certainty. We still publish the digits, of course. Ellis has probably framed his.

Ellis earned 71 closest-score bonuses, six more than me and thirteen more than Rowan. The bonus uses the combined absolute error on both teams’ scores; tied closest forecasts each receive it. He picked fewer winners than the top three writers but kept more losing and winning calls near the eventual score. That distinction matters when judging what each forecast got right.
Rowan’s Saffron pick survives the entire bracket

Rowan picked Saffron 30–27 over Mossdeep when the fourteen-team postseason field opened. He had both finalists and the champion. Saffron then won four straight, including road revenge at Mt. Silver and the neutral-site rematch with Mossdeep. All three regular-season Psi Corps defeats had come away from home by a combined seven points. Rowan treated those narrow losses as evidence that Saffron could beat the top seeds. The playoff result supports him.

My original bracket advanced twelve correct round winners out of thirteen, and it had all thirteen actual matchups. That includes Blackthorn beating Cinnabar in the wild card, a result that wrecked several other brackets. Rowan and Tessa each advanced ten correct round winners, Ellis and Dorian eight. This grade credits the right team winning a round even if the forecast had a different opponent. The weekly playoff picks were separate forecasts made as the actual matchups arrived.

Rowan’s final-week score moved to Saffron 35–28. He got the seven-point margin exactly and overshot both scores by eleven. Dorian’s Saffron 27–24 was the closest championship prediction, ten combined points away. Every writer predicted more points from both teams than the final produced. The final’s turnovers, injury and defensive stands supplied a stronger restraint than any of our scorelines allowed.
Five writers answer for their season

Tessa’s strongest result is the one she would insist on checking across all 221 games. She won the weekly table while refusing to turn every close result into proof that a club had transformed. Her championship miss came from expecting Mossdeep’s offensive continuity to hold. BeckhmJr’s exit and two lost scoring chances exposed how much that continuity could matter within a single game. Her final coaching ballot, Gardenia at Eterna, remains a useful invitation to discuss what eleven wins with 214 points required.

Rowan spent most of the season ranking Mossdeep first and still picked Saffron to win the title. That was a distinction between the strongest completed regular season and the club he wanted in a championship matchup. He can now make it loudly. His rankings also caught the league’s upper end: the final regular-season top four reached the conference finals, and the top two reached the Bowl. He moved Hearthome from thirtieth on the first board to fourteenth at the end. The late climb was necessary and earned.

Ellis had the lowest appetite for declaring a club finished after a bad afternoon. Lavender rewarded that patience by turning 4–5 into a division title. Mahogany’s 5–11–1 record and minus-twelve differential gave him a season-long reason to distrust standings without examining close games. His original bracket sent Cinnabar past Lavender and into the Bowl against Mossdeep. Blackthorn ended that idea immediately. Sympathy for a season’s arc still has to meet the next opponent.

Dorian selected Mt. Silver over Sunyshore in his opening championship bracket. Neither finalist arrived. He then picked Saffron correctly in the actual Bowl and came closest to its score. That adjustment deserves credit, with the original bracket left intact beside it. His weekly record finished last among the five writers, and none of his six awards selections matched the official winners. He will argue that a ballot is an argument. I agree. Arguments can also lose six decisions in a row.

My own best work came in the playoff matchups before the final. My weakest shared assumption came on the MVP ballot. Four of us voted for Marino. Three of us also chose BeckhmJr as the best offensive player. The league gave both awards to the receiver. I understood what 32 receiving touchdowns meant and still treated the quarterback as the default choice for the larger award. That deserves reconsideration before next season’s ballots.
What the final rankings got right and what moved

Mossdeep held first place from Week 5 through the Week 20 contender board. Saffron finished the regular season second, followed by Mt. Silver, Sunyshore and Cinnabar. The conference championship field matched the top four. The fifth-ranked Blaze then offer the warning against treating a final board as a playoff result: Blackthorn beat them 38–10 in the wild-card rematch after Exploud’s finale injury.

Hearthome’s rise from thirtieth to fourteenth was the largest of the notable recoveries. Celadon climbed from twenty-ninth to eighteenth, Pewter from twenty-eighth to nineteenth, and Mauville from twenty-fourth to sixteenth. Canalave moved the other way, seventh to twenty-second; Cerulean fell from tenth to twenty-fourth. Those changes were based on games that happened. The next board will need to account for retirements, additions and a fresh season rather than carrying every finishing position forward by habit.

The championship is Saffron’s. Tessa won the weekly picks, Rowan picked the champion early, Ellis led the closest-score count, Dorian got nearest to the final score and I took twelve opening-bracket winners into the last game. The archived scorelines remain available with the weeks in which we published them.

articles.title: BeckhmJr’s final ends early as the league turns to offseason recovery
articles.dek: The complete 51-player comparison, the injuries that shaped the last weeks and the roster departures already confirmed.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Accel BeckhmJr’s first-quarter exit changed the Indigo Bowl and left Mossdeep trying to recover from two first-half turnovers without its leading receiver. He caught one pass for ten yards in the 24–17 defeat. The current injury report lists nineteen weeks. That is the recorded recovery counter at the opening of the offseason; it is not a schedule of Season 2 games he will miss.

The distinction matters now because the league has moved into its staff phase, with re-signing, free agency and the draft still ahead. Offseason recovery must be confirmed as those stages advance. A number carried over from the final does not establish a diagnosis, a surgery timetable or a return date. Mossdeep needs the next availability update before it can make claims about the receiver’s opening-day status.

The football consequence in the final is much clearer. BeckhmJr had led the regular season with 1,953 receiving yards and 32 receiving touchdowns. Derrat Brooks took nine targets and caught five passes for 94 yards against Saffron. Ninjulio Jones added 84, Ninjaskamara 72 and a late touchdown, and Driflon Diggs scored on a six-yard catch. Mossdeep found replacement production while losing the player who had supplied its largest scoring advantage all year.
Recovery counters at the start of the offseason

The table compares the report before the final with the report after it. It includes every player with an injury entry in either report, including players whose counter has reached zero. Zero means the current report no longer carries a positive recovery counter. It does not erase the earlier injury or imply a separate medical examination. A dash means no injury entry was present in that report.

Among the longer remaining counters are Cerulean linebacker Watchog at thirteen weeks, Sunyshore’s 88 Special at twelve and Mt. Silver quarterback Crem Ftzpatrik at nine. Their clubs have different roster questions, but each needs an updated offseason report before converting those numbers into availability plans. The same rule applies to BeckhmJr’s nineteen: the next league stage can change the status.

Vermilion’s Drakloak has a five-week entry after leading the club with 755 regular-season receiving yards, although the current roster lists the player at cornerback. Olivine’s Gabite has four weeks after a 702-yard rushing season, and Mauville’s leading rusher Unfezant has three. Listed position and the work a player actually performed are both relevant when describing who must cover an absence.

Mossdeep’s report also carries Poury Holt at two weeks. Flock Purdy, Ninjaskamara and Champ Baeley have zero-week entries. Those names belong in the comparison even though the positive counters differ. The final’s new problem is BeckhmJr; the complete table keeps it in the context of the league’s remaining injuries.
Retirement creates a different kind of opening

Twenty-six players assigned to clubs before the final have retired. Those departures are permanent roster changes, unlike a recovery counter awaiting the offseason’s next update. Mossdeep loses Luvrelle Revis after thirteen regular-season starts. Lavender loses EARTHQUAKE!!! and Mr. Joe, who combined for 33 starts. Sunyshore loses safety @mped UP after seventeen appearances. Each club must replace work that was performed throughout the season.

Sootopolis loses first-team All-League safety Pachirisu and reserve linebacker Mawile. Viridian loses linebackers Wigglytuff and Volbeat, who started fourteen and seventeen games respectively. Dewford loses Ambipom and Kricketune, taking eleven and seven starts out of its linebacker group. These are immediate areas to examine before the draft, even where the rest of a roster remains competitive.

Across the whole player pool, 74 players newly have retired status; 48 were already unattached before the Bowl. The 26 club departures are the useful count for this issue’s team outlooks. Listing all retirements as new losses to current rosters would overstate the disruption.
The next availability update

The staff stage is the current checkpoint. Contracts, free agency and the draft will alter the depth around injured or retired players, and the subsequent recovery update will establish which injury entries remain relevant. There are no posted upcoming games to preview in this issue. We will carry the confirmed departures forward and revisit the injury counters when the league advances.

For Mossdeep, the immediate sporting fact remains painful and specific: its MVP played only briefly in a championship decided by one touchdown. His season awards recognize what he accomplished before that afternoon. His next availability report will answer a different question.
