articles.title: Kanto–Johto after the title: sixteen teams and their next decisions
articles.dek: A complete club-by-club season review, including every team that missed the playoffs. Records and scoring totals below are regular-season figures unless labeled otherwise.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Saffron finished the conference’s work by winning the Indigo Bowl. The other fifteen clubs enter an offseason shaped by very different evidence: Mt. Silver’s lost rematch, Lavender’s veteran departures, Cinnabar’s abrupt finish and several rebuilding teams with useful individual seasons. I want each review to preserve what the club actually achieved while identifying work the next roster can address.

Each heading carries the seventeen-game regular-season record. The completed playoff result is included in the club review. Offseason priorities are editorial assessments; signings and draft choices remain ahead.
Saffron Psi Corps · 14–3

Manning's 4,633 passing yards, Lamb's 1,878 receiving yards and two 20-sack edge rushers powered the second-ranked scoring offense and scoring defense. A 70–0 rout of 12-win Blackthorn put its upper end on the record. The club then won four playoff games, including the rematches with both No. 1 seeds, to finish 18–3 overall.

The champions have earned continuity where it helped them most: Manning’s accurate passing, Lamb’s receiving volume and a rush that can make a good offense spend downs recovering. Their final also showed the value of Pickens and Irving when the defense concentrated on the headline names. An offseason plan should protect those complementary opportunities. Four playoff wins establish the quality of this team. Keeping enough depth to play four more is a more useful objective than assuming the trophy makes every roster decision easy.
Mt. Silver Reds · 14–3

Started 6–0, beat Saffron 36–33 and earned the first seed on head-to-head. Lynch had 1,200 rushing yards in 11 games. Closed with losses at Cinnabar and at home to Cianwood around the Azalea win, then won the divisional round before losing the Saffron rematch. Crem Ftzpatrik's nine-week injury entry and Medicham's retirement matter at different levels of the depth chart.

Lynch’s workload remains the first thing I would examine. Eleven appearances produced the league’s leading rushing total, an extraordinary return and a reason to have a dependable alternative when he is unavailable. The quarterback availability picture also needs another report before camp expectations harden. Connor McLarren beat Saffron once and lost the game that decided the conference. That split supplies plenty of material for his usual conversation; the roster work should concentrate on sustaining the offense through the next interruption.
Cinnabar Blaze · 12–5

Beat Blackthorn 31–19 and Mt. Silver 38–24 during a four-win finish. Blackthorn won the immediate playoff rematch 38–10 after Exploud's finale injury. Gholdengo threw for 3,867, while rookie Tatsugiri's five INT came in a first-team All-League season.

The final four regular-season wins justified confidence, and the wild-card defeat justified a close examination of how much changed when Exploud became unavailable. Gholdengo’s passing and Tatsugiri’s coverage give Blaine established players on both sides. The next additions should make that structure less vulnerable to losing one contributor. Blackthorn won the rematch by four touchdowns; treating it only as a strange afternoon would miss a useful test of the roster’s alternatives when the preferred plan cannot carry the game.
Blackthorn Dragons · 12–5

Hatterene threw for 4,532. The Dragons beat Mt. Silver 30–22 in the regular season and forced a one-possession divisional finish there, 21–14. They were fifth in points and 27th in points allowed. The 70–0 loss at Saffron, one-point division loss at Lavender and 38–10 win at Cinnabar outline the range.

The Dragons can point to a playoff road win and a seven-point divisional defeat as evidence that their ceiling was real. They can also look at 348 regular-season points allowed and understand why the season swung so sharply. Hatterene’s passing gives the offense a reason to keep attacking. I would direct the offseason toward preventing ordinary possessions from becoming scoring chances, so another productive passing day does not require an immediate answer after every defensive series.
Lavender Wails · 12–5

A 4–5 start became eight straight wins, culminating in 21–20 over Blackthorn to take the division. The Wails won all six one-score regular games and beat Vermilion 24–21 before losing to Saffron. EARTHQUAKE!!! and Mr. Joe retire after a combined 33 regular-season starts; this is a genuine front-seven rebuild.

Travis Scarboro’s division title came from a long recovery, and the six close-game wins required dependable work late in games. Replacing two veteran front-seven players with 33 combined starts will test that dependability immediately. I would expect the draft discussion to return to who can take those snaps. The Wails have proved they can keep a season alive after a poor opening. They would make the next one easier by reducing the number of afternoons that need a perfect final possession.
Vermilion Volts · 10–7

Opened 10–9 over eventual champion Saffron, won its final three regular-season games by seven, three and three and was 8–1 in one-score games. Lavender ended the playoff run with a 24–21 win. Volbeat recorded 14 sacks. Victreebel retires after 17 starts, and 755-yard receiver Drakloak has a five-week injury entry and is listed at CB in the current export.

Eight wins in nine one-score games helped Vermilion turn 210 points into ten victories. That performance deserves acknowledgment, but it also leaves a thin cushion for the next season. Victreebel’s retirement removes seventeen starts from the roster. Drakloak’s recovery and actual offensive role need to be settled as the lineup changes. Vermilion beat the eventual champion on opening day; they should seek a more reliable weekly way to produce points than hoping every close finish lands on their side again.
Olivine Ironclads · 9–8

Ninth-fewest allowed and a 12-sack Darmanitan produced playoff football. A 17–0 finale at Azalea held off Cianwood after the direct loss the previous week. Gabite's 702 rushing yards and four-week injury entry anchor the offseason backfield question. Saffron beat the Ironclads 42–10.

Olivine’s defense supplied a credible playoff base, and Darmanitan’s twelve sacks earned second-team honors. The attack has farther to move after scoring 220 points. Gabite’s recovery matters because the backfield accounted for a substantial share of the club’s dependable production. The 42–10 playoff loss at Saffron showed the difficulty of chasing a top passing offense. Adding another way to sustain possessions would support the defense and give the Ironclads more freedom when the early score goes against them.
Cianwood Crushers · 8–9

Climbed from 31st in Week 9 to 15th on the final board. Beat Olivine 10–3 and Mt. Silver 21–13 on the road to close. Bibarel rushed for 1,087 yards and Leafeon had 9.5 sacks. Sixth-fewest points allowed alongside the 19th-ranked scoring total puts pass production in focus.

The closing road wins at Olivine and Mt. Silver should give Cianwood confidence in its defense and rushing base. Bibarel passed a thousand yards, while Leafeon earned first-team recognition on the other side. The offense’s nineteenth-ranked scoring output is where a new passing option could make the largest practical difference. Chuck’s team does not need to abandon its identity to win another two games. It needs enough complementary production that a successful afternoon on the ground can create a lead worth protecting.
Violet Falcons · 8–9

Beat Sunyshore 33–20 on the road, then lost its final two games 51–10 to Lavender and 27–13 to Mahogany. Iron Jugulis threw for 3,371 and Milotic picked off five. Delibird retires after nine games. The defense allowed 314 points despite 8 wins.

Violet demonstrated a high ceiling at Sunyshore and then surrendered 78 points over its final two games. That sequence directs attention toward defensive consistency rather than another claim that the team can beat anyone on a given day. Iron Jugulis’s passing and Milotic’s interceptions provide something to build around. Delibird’s retirement opens another roster job. The next additions should make the difficult weeks less damaging, because eight wins leave little room to recover when consecutive defensive performances end the season early.
Cerulean Tide · 7–10

Beat 13-win Sunyshore 12–6 and 12-win Cinnabar 18–17. A three-loss finish cost momentum. Farigiraf threw for 3,532, while the leading rusher had 224 yards and OLB Watchog carries a 13-week injury entry. Scoring defense was 30th.

A leading rusher with 224 yards leaves the passing game carrying too much of the offense’s ordinary work. Farigiraf produced 3,532 passing yards, and Cerulean still scored only 240 points. Watchog’s recovery is another matter to follow as the defense tries to improve from thirtieth in points allowed. The wins over Sunyshore and Cinnabar keep the season from being dismissed outright. They also make the lack of a dependable weekly plan more frustrating: the Tide showed possibilities they could not sustain.
Celadon Bloom · 6–11

Recovered from 1–5 over the first six weeks to rise from No. 29 to No. 18. Eighth-fewest allowed, but 2–6 in one-score games. Rookie Ponyta had 672 receiving yards, Klawf had 10 sacks, and 17-start OLB Seaking retires. Seaking also led the rushing with 645 yards; the retirement removes work on both sides.

Celadon’s defense allowed fewer points than all but seven clubs, while the offense finished with 207. Ponyta’s rookie receiving contribution is a useful place to start adding support. Seaking’s retirement removes a full season of starting linebacker work, so the defense cannot be treated as self-maintaining. The 2–6 close-game record suggests a few better offensive possessions could have changed the standings substantially. Erika also needs to replace Seaking’s 645 rushing yards, because the retiring linebacker supplied the club’s leading rushing total as well.
Pewter Rockers · 6–11

Seventh-fewest allowed and league-low scoring, with 13 one-score games. Delcatty rushed for 953 and Iron Leaves recorded nine sacks. The Rockers beat Vermilion 17–9 and lost the finale 13–7 to Cinnabar. Froslass retires after 12 starts.

Delcatty’s 953 rushing yards and Iron Leaves’s nine sacks give Pewter two productive players to work with. The league-low 181 points are still the first problem to solve. Thirteen one-score games made most weeks competitive, but competitiveness produced only six wins. Froslass’s retirement adds a defensive replacement job. I would judge the offensive additions by whether they can create a second dependable path to points when the run game stalls, rather than by another collection of close losses that looked respectable.
Mahogany Frost · 5–11–1

A minus-12 differential came with 2–9–1 in eight-point games. Shut out Blackthorn 21–0 in Week 2 and swept Violet. Dugtrio reached 800 receiving yards, Bruxish had 15 sacks and Lopunny intercepted seven. Gastrodon retires after starting every game at FB.

A 2–9–1 record in one-score games is a painful way to turn a minus-twelve differential into only five victories. Dugtrio, Bruxish and Lopunny produced enough receiving, sacks and interceptions to justify retaining the useful parts. Gastrodon’s retirement removes a full season at fullback. Mahogany should review the actual late possessions behind those losses while replacing that blocking work. The record can improve without the team becoming unrecognizable, but close losses do not correct themselves simply because the arithmetic looks unfair.
Viridian Titans · 5–12

Opened with a 14–10 road upset of Cinnabar, had 1,126 rushing yards from Gabite and a league-best 11 INT from Sigilyph. Finished the last six calendar weeks 1–5. ILB Wigglytuff (14 starts) and OLB Volbeat (17) retire, leaving two established linebacker jobs.

Gabite’s 1,126 rushing yards and Sigilyph’s eleven interceptions are substantial individual seasons inside a five-win team. The retirement of two starting linebackers now makes the middle of the defense an immediate concern. Wigglytuff and Volbeat combined for 31 starts that must be redistributed. The offense also needs to get more points from its rushing production. Giovanni has useful players on both sides; the offseason’s challenge is to connect those isolated strengths through enough dependable snaps to stop another late-season slide.
Azalea Swarm · 5–12

Reached No. 21 in Week 13 with earlier close wins over Rustboro and Olivine and then lost five straight. Pyroar caught 618 receiving yards, Drampa threw for 2,669 and Zoroark made second-team All-League. Azalea scored 182, one above the league low.

Azalea finished one point above the league’s lowest scoring total and lost five straight to close. Pyroar’s receiving and Zoroark’s second-team recognition give the club individual successes, but they did not produce a sustainable weekly advantage. Drampa’s 2,669 passing yards leave room for another reliable target and improved offensive execution. The earlier close wins over Rustboro and Olivine are useful examples to study. They should inform additions that make those possessions repeatable rather than stand as the season’s entire case for optimism.
Fuchsia Shadows · 3–14

Started 0–6 and finished with five losses, with a 3–3 stretch in between. Empoleon passed for 3,434 and Heatmor had 850 receiving yards, giving the club more passing production than the W–L record suggests. Lost eight of ten close games. Every-game starter Seaking retires at OLB.

Empoleon’s 3,434 passing yards and Heatmor’s 850 receiving yards show that Fuchsia could move the ball despite finishing last. The next additions must make that production more useful on the scoreboard and reduce the 387 points conceded. Seaking’s retirement opens a full-time outside-linebacker job. Holding the projected first pick gives the Shadows a choice between several approaches rather than a guaranteed cure. They should take a player who can perform a demanding assignment early and build a more coherent roster around that contribution.

articles.title: Hoenn–Sinnoh after Mossdeep’s near-perfect season: all sixteen offseason outlooks
articles.dek: A complete club-by-club season review, including every team that missed the playoffs. Records and scoring totals below are regular-season figures unless labeled otherwise.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Mossdeep finished 19–1 and one touchdown short of the championship. Sunyshore pushed the Eclipse in the conference final; the rest of the conference now has a full season of evidence about the gap. The sixteen reviews below separate established production from the additions and recovery updates still needed before another season begins.

Each heading carries the seventeen-game regular-season record. The completed playoff result is included in the club review. Offseason priorities are editorial assessments; signings and draft choices remain ahead.
Mossdeep Eclipse · 17–0

Beat Saffron 20–17 in Week 10 and Sunyshore 27–3 in Week 16. Allowed six points in its last three regular-season games. Marino threw 4,341 yards and 56 TD with four interceptions before the playoffs. Beat Dewford 40–3 and Sunyshore 37–31, then finished 19–1 overall. Luvrelle Revis retires after 13 starts and BeckhmJr's final-week injury gives the club two offseason roster questions.

The next roster review has to preserve what made the offense exceptional while providing credible answers when a starter leaves a game. Brooks’s receiving work in the final demonstrated willingness and production under pressure; it also showed how far an emergency can move a player from his usual job. Revis’s retirement creates an immediate defensive vacancy. I would judge the offseason by who can perform those actual assignments, alongside the recovery update on BeckhmJr, before treating another perfect regular season as the expected starting point.
Sunyshore Starseekers · 13–4

Beat Lavender and Blackthorn on the road and lost both Mossdeep meetings, taking the second to 37–31 after playing two playoff rounds. Fifth-fewest points allowed. Fera LaGatr led with 766 receiving yards. The club loses 17-game safety @mped UP to retirement. 88 Special has a 12-week injury entry.

Karson Jones reached the conference final with an offense that could challenge Mossdeep far more seriously in the rematch. Replacing @mped UP’s full-season safety work is the clearest confirmed vacancy. The longer health entry for 88 Special makes offensive depth another area to revisit as the offseason advances. The Starseekers can reasonably believe they are close to the top. Their acquisitions should help them survive the difficult possessions that decided the conference final rather than merely reproduce a good regular-season box score.
Petalburg Pride · 12–5

Went 10–2 in one-score games and beat Rustboro in all three meetings, 29–23 in the playoffs. Oinkologne ran for 957 regular-season yards. The 24–10 loss at Sunyshore ended a season that produced 12 wins with a minus-six differential. Dustox retires after 13 appearances.

Ten wins in twelve one-score games deserve credit for execution and caution about how often the margin can be repeated. Oinkologne’s production supplies an offensive foundation. The next improvement should make a good game easier to finish before the last possession, whether through another reliable scoring option or stronger coverage. Dustox’s departure adds a defined job to fill. Petalburg’s three victories over Rustboro were earned; its minus-six season differential still leaves substantial room to make the next playoff team more convincing.
Dewford Breakers · 11–6

Won its last three regular games, including 35–29 at Rustboro, then beat Eterna 20–9 before losing 40–3 at Mossdeep. Gliscor picked off six and Excadrill ran for 708. OLB Ambipom (11 starts) and Kricketune (seven) retire together.

The linebacker departures give Dewford a specific draft problem after a season that included both a road playoff win and a decisive loss at Mossdeep. Gliscor’s interceptions helped finish possessions; replacing Ambipom and Kricketune means finding players who can keep those opportunities available. The 40–3 divisional result is a benchmark for the distance to the conference’s best offense. The club can build from eleven regular-season wins while being exact about which defensive work now lacks an incumbent.
Eterna Thorns · 11–6

Third-fewest allowed and 23rd scoring. Beat Sunyshore 14–6 and Petalburg 20–14, but put up nine in both the regular finale and wild card. Stantler ran for 661 and Cramorant caught 542 yards. The season points to a need for more scoring flexibility.

Gardenia’s team allowed only 184 points and still had little room for an offensive mistake. The next useful addition should give the attack another way to move the chains when Stantler’s rushing or the first receiving option is contained. Cramorant’s 542 yards led the receivers, a modest ceiling for an eleven-win club. Eterna already knows how to keep opponents within reach. Scoring nine points in each of its last two games makes a stronger passing contribution the most direct route to advancement.
Rustboro Stone · 9–8

Won 41–38 against Cinnabar and 37–21 at Dewford. The Stone then lost three closing games by exactly seven, six and six across regular and playoffs, including two against Petalburg. Philly Gabite (870 rush yards) and Gibby Timmy (953 receiving yards) led a No. 7 scoring offense. Watchog retires after 16 games.

Tyler Scarboro has productive offensive pieces in Philly Gabite and Gibby Timmy. He also has three recent defeats against Petalburg to inspect without hunting for a hypothetical opponent. The next acquisitions should help the Stone convert that scoring ability into firmer control of a game, with Watchog’s retirement adding one confirmed opening. A seven-point loss followed by two six-point losses leaves useful, specific situations to review. The roster does not need a speech about wanting it more; it needs better answers in those possessions.
Hearthome Haunts · 8–8–1

Rose from Week 13's No. 28 with a five-win finish and overtook Mauville for the last seed. Frosmoth threw for 3,101 yards. Sunyshore beat the Haunts for a third time, 23–6 in the playoffs. First-team Swampert is a useful independent roster anchor.

The five-win finish changed what this team could reasonably expect from its offseason. Frosmoth’s 3,101 passing yards and Swampert’s first-team recognition are identifiable pieces to retain around. The three losses to Sunyshore identify an equally useful obstacle. Hearthome reached the field by improving over time; the next step is to carry that late competence into September and add enough offensive variety to challenge a division opponent that saw the same roster repeatedly and kept finding a winning answer.
Mauville Dynamos · 8–9

Held Rustboro and Snowpoint scoreless in wins, but closed with close losses at Dewford and Petalburg. OLB Volbeat's 13 rookie sacks and Mothim's 733 receiving yards provide two building blocks. Reserve HB Wigglytuff retired and leading rusher Unfezant has a three-week injury entry.

The Dynamos have a rookie award winner in Volbeat and an All-League receiving contributor in Mothim. Those are unusually clear starting points for an eight-win team. The closing losses to Dewford and Petalburg made the playoff miss hurt, but they also establish the standard for the next improvement. I would look for another reliable offensive contributor while checking Unfezant’s recovery. Wigglytuff’s retirement leaves a smaller vacancy than some clubs face, giving Mauville a chance to add quality without rebuilding an entire position group.
Canalave Bulwark · 8–9

Dropped from seventh to 22nd after going 1–5 over Weeks 13–18. Gabite ran for 800, Passimian had 10 sacks and Weezing made first-team All-League. Retiring FB Ariados started 12 games. Two RBs carry positive injury counters and scoring ranked 30th.

Canalave’s 1–5 closing stretch and 183 points show how thoroughly the offense ran out of useful answers. Gabite’s 800 rushing yards deserve support from a passing game that can punish attention to the backfield. Ariados’s retirement also removes an experienced blocker from that structure. Weezing and Passimian offer proven defensive work, so the offseason does not begin without strengths. It begins with an attack that must produce enough for those strengths to matter beyond another low-scoring near miss.
Sootopolis Surge · 7–10

Drampa threw for 3,169 and Kingdra had six interceptions. The Surge upset Vermilion 24–10 and closed 17–16 over Fortree. All-League safety Pachirisu started all 17 and retires, along with reserve MLB Mawile. Sootopolis allowed the fifth-most points.

Replacing Pachirisu is a substantial task because the retiring safety played every game and earned first-team honors. Kingdra’s six interceptions are encouraging, but the 354 points allowed show that takeaways alone did not hold the defense together. Mawile’s departure adds depth work at linebacker. Drampa’s passing gives the attack a baseline from which to improve. I would prioritize reliable defensive snaps and communication before reading the final one-point win as proof that the larger scoring-prevention problem had already been solved.
Lavaridge Inferno · 7–10

Beat division winner Petalburg 35–21 and Eterna 20–13 away, yet its defense surrendered 355. Venusaur's eight INT and Maractus's 11.5 sacks show where proven disruption already exists. Mossdeep shut out the Inferno 27–0 in the finale.

Venusaur’s eight interceptions and Maractus’s 11.5 sacks show that Lavaridge had players capable of ending drives. Allowing 355 points shows how much happened between those plays. The offseason should add dependable coverage and defensive support around that disruption. The home win over Petalburg and road win at Eterna demonstrate that the club could compete with playoff teams; the home finale against Mossdeep demonstrated the distance to the conference leader. Flannery needs a roster that makes the first version of the Inferno appear more consistently.
Veilstone Fists · 6–11

Ponyta and Vigoroth supply 750 receiving and 807 rushing yards from the rookie class. Played 11 close games and beat Hearthome early. Its 29th-ranked scoring points and the retirement of 17-game OLB Sandslash leave work on both sides.

Ponyta’s rookie award and Vigoroth’s 807 rushing yards give Veilstone a young foundation more encouraging than its twenty-ninth-ranked scoring total. The next offensive work should help those players sustain drives together. Sandslash’s retirement simultaneously removes a seventeen-game linebacker, so the club has a clear defensive vacancy for the draft. Eleven close games show how frequently a manageable improvement might have mattered. The opportunity is to turn useful rookie production into a complete weekly offense while replacing a large defensive workload.
Pastoria Waves · 6–11

Beat eventual division winners Lavender 17–7 and Eterna 10–3, then finished with four losses. Kilowattrel had 603 receiving yards, Banette 11 sacks, Dubwool four INT. Safety Azumarill retires after 17 appearances and 14 starts.

Pastoria beat Lavender and Eterna, then lost its last four games. Kilowattrel, Banette and Dubwool supplied receiving, pressure and interception production, but those contributions did not combine into enough consistent scoring or prevention. Azumarill’s retirement takes fourteen starts out of the safety group. I would begin the defensive additions there, while looking for another offensive answer beyond the leading receiver’s 603 yards. The successful games establish that the roster has workable pieces; the finishing stretch establishes how much support those pieces need.
Snowpoint Blizzard · 4–13

Demolished Canalave 35–0 in Week 2, lost five straight to close and was 2–7 in one-score games. Oinkologne ran for 943 and Drakloak caught 732 receiving yards. Safety Medicham retires after 13 starts.

Oinkologne’s 943 rushing yards and Drakloak’s 732 receiving yards supplied genuine production, even as Snowpoint lost its last five. Medicham’s retirement creates a safety opening after thirteen starts. A 2–7 record in close games makes the final standings harsher than some individual afternoons looked, but the club still has to improve what happened in those endings. The draft can help both the new defensive vacancy and the need for more complete possessions around the established offensive contributors.
Oreburgh Miners · 4–13

Was 3–9 in one-score games, including a 15–10 loss to Eterna followed by a 14–10 finale win over Canalave. Drednaw's 11.5 sacks and first-team recognition supply a proven defensive piece. Safety Medicham has a short injury entry and is a different player from the retiring Snowpoint Medicham.

Drednaw’s first-team season gives Oreburgh a defender worth building around. The Miners won only three of twelve close games, including a late narrow loss to Eterna before beating Canalave. Those results support a detailed look at the offense’s decision-making and support for its quarterback. A high first-round pick creates options, which Calvin explores in his mock. The objective should be a roster that can finish a tight game more reliably, while preserving the pass-rush production that already gives it a chance.
Fortree Skyhawks · 4–13

Went 0–6 within the division and conceded a league-high 413 points. Beat playoff Vermilion 34–10 and lost two closing division games by a combined five. Rabsca threw for 2,857, and Toxapex made second-team All-League. Mawile retires after 17 appearances.

Fortree scored 251 points, a much more workable total than the league-high 413 it allowed. Toxapex’s second-team season offers one defensive anchor, and Mawile’s retirement creates another position to fill. The Skyhawks lost every divisional game, so offseason progress has a clear test against familiar opponents. The two closing division defeats were narrow, but the full defensive total demands more than a claim that the team was close. Better protection and stronger defensive support would both help Rabsca’s offense stay competitive longer.

articles.title: The final Pecking Order: Saffron takes first, all 32 clubs get a season verdict
articles.dek: Rowan closes the Season 1 board with the champion on top and a complete league assessment before the draft.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Saffron is first. Four postseason wins ended with a 24–17 victory over the team I had ranked first since Week 5. Mossdeep’s regular season remains the best in the league; the championship supplies the decisive new result. I picked the Psi Corps to win the title when the playoffs opened and will now exercise admirable restraint by mentioning it only as often as space permits.

This is the final Season 1 assessment, including the postseason. It is not a forecast of the roster that will exist after free agency and the draft. The order weighs the whole season, with the latest playoff results carrying particular force among teams that met. The club reviews elsewhere in the issue address offseason work in more detail. Here are all 32 final verdicts.

rankings.text: Four playoff wins, two top-seed rematches settled and a championship earned with the ball secured. Tare’s four sacks and Lamb’s 153 yards settled the final board. I picked this champion before the playoffs, which will be appearing in my correspondence for a while. Saffron finishes first because it completed the hardest work in the league.

Nineteen wins and one defeat leave an exceptional season with an exceptionally painful ending. The first-quarter loss of BeckhmJr and two first-half turnovers put the final beyond a late recovery. Mossdeep still produced the league’s best regular-season offense and defense. Second place records the championship result without pretending the other nineteen games disappeared.

The regular-season head-to-head win earned the top seed; the rematch sent Saffron to the Bowl. Lynch’s 1,200 rushing yards in eleven games remain absurdly productive. Mt. Silver finishes third with a genuine contender’s season and an offseason that needs to protect its offensive continuity. Connor McLarren can supply his own comment about how close this was.

The Starseekers made Mossdeep defend a six-point conference-final margin after losing the regular meeting 27–3. That is a meaningful improvement against the hardest opponent in the conference. Karson Jones has a safety job to replace after @mped UP’s retirement. Fourth recognizes the postseason run; the next step is winning that final possession against the top two.

A 38–10 wild-card win at Cinnabar moves Blackthorn ahead of the Blaze, and a 21–14 loss at Mt. Silver keeps the finish respectable. Hatterene threw for 4,532 regular-season yards. The defense allowed 348 points and once lost 70–0. Readers requesting a tidy one-sentence description of this team should contact someone with fewer actual results in front of them.

The Wails turned 4–5 into a division title and a playoff victory. Six wins in six close regular-season games were a considerable achievement, with rather less spare room than Travis Scarboro would prefer. The retirement of EARTHQUAKE!!! and Mr. Joe now demands real replacements. Sixth rewards the completed recovery before next season asks the front seven to introduce itself.

The four-win regular-season finish included Mt. Silver and Blackthorn. The immediate playoff rematch ended 38–10 in the wrong direction after Exploud’s finale injury. I am moving the Blaze below the teams that advanced past them while retaining respect for Gholdengo’s season and Tatsugiri’s first-team award. The ending exposed a depth problem the late winning streak had not solved.

Petalburg beat Rustboro three times and won a playoff game. Ten victories in twelve close regular-season games helped a minus-six differential produce a 12–5 record. The Pride earned those wins; I would like next season’s offense to leave fewer of them awaiting the last possession. Oinkologne’s 957 rushing yards provide a sensible place to begin that improvement.

The Eterna road win was a solid playoff result. The 40–3 defeat at Mossdeep was a very different examination. Dewford finishes in the top ten after eleven regular-season wins, with Gliscor’s six interceptions among its defensive strengths. Losing Ambipom and Kricketune to retirement gives the draft discussion a specific linebacking workload to replace.

Gibby Timmy made first-team All-League and the offense ranked seventh in points. Rustboro still lost its final three games across regular season and playoffs by seven, six and six. Two were against Petalburg, which leaves Tyler Scarboro plenty of familiar tape. Tenth reflects an attack good enough to compete and a team that could not finish the important close games.

Eleven wins on 214 points demanded an excellent defense, and Eterna allowed only 184. Nine points in the regular finale and nine in the playoff loss show the ceiling of that arrangement. Gardenia deserves credit for the season. The offseason deserves another offensive option, preferably one who makes a fourteen-point deficit feel less like a lengthy administrative hearing.

A playoff berth and the ninth-best scoring defense give Olivine a respectable finish. Saffron’s 42–10 wild-card win showed how difficult catching a leading passing offense could become. Darmanitan’s twelve sacks earned second-team recognition. Gabite’s recovery and the offense around him need attention before the Ironclads can expect their next postseason appearance to last longer.

The team that beat Saffron 10–9 on opening day finished with ten regular-season wins and a 24–21 playoff defeat. Eight wins in nine close regular games explain how 210 points went so far. I have been unkind about the scoring total; the record deserves its credit. Replacing Victreebel’s seventeen starts and improving the offense are now both necessary.

A five-win finish dragged Hearthome from the lower reaches of my board into the playoffs. Sunyshore then beat the Haunts for the third time. Frosmoth’s passing and Swampert’s first-team award give the offseason a foundation beyond the late winning streak. I had this club thirtieth in Week 4. Fourteenth is a substantial correction I am happy to print.

Cianwood won at Olivine and Mt. Silver to close, finishing with the sixth-fewest points allowed. Bibarel supplied 1,087 rushing yards and Leafeon first-team defensive recognition. An 8–9 season can still contain a useful late direction. The passing contribution needs to support that rushing and defensive base if next year’s final-week wins are going to extend a playoff season.

Volbeat won the defensive rookie award and Mothim made second-team All-League. Those are tangible reasons to like Mauville beyond a general impression that it was nearly there. Close closing losses kept the Dynamos out at 8–9. Another offensive contributor and an updated report on Unfezant would make the offseason more useful than another discussion of the final standings.

The road win at Sunyshore remains a good result. The 78 points allowed in the final two games remain on the same schedule. Iron Jugulis threw for 3,371 yards and Milotic intercepted five passes, so there are productive players to support. Seventeenth puts the eight-win club ahead of the thinner records while acknowledging how badly the finish weakened its case.

Celadon recovered from a 1–5 opening, allowed the eighth-fewest points and still finished 6–11. The 2–6 close-game record directs attention to an offense that scored 207. Ponyta’s 672 receiving yards are a useful rookie contribution. Seaking’s retirement means the defense also has a full-time job to replace before Erika can concentrate exclusively on adding points.

The defense ranked seventh in points allowed; the offense ranked last in points scored. That split produced thirteen close games and six wins. Delcatty’s 953 rushing yards deserve another dependable scoring partner. Pewter finishes nineteenth because its defense kept it competitive, with the understanding that another season of honorable 13–7 defeats will exhaust even my supply of qualified compliments.

Five wins, eleven losses, one tie and only twelve more points allowed than scored. A 2–9–1 close-game record explains much of the misery. Dugtrio, Bruxish and Lopunny supplied useful production, and Gastrodon now leaves a fullback vacancy. Twentieth respects the underlying competitiveness without converting the nine close losses into victories that never happened.

The Inferno beat playoff club Petalburg at home and won at Eterna. They also allowed 355 points and ended with a home shutout loss to Mossdeep. Venusaur’s eight interceptions and Maractus’s 11.5 sacks give the defense proven disruption. The next improvement needs to come on the snaps between those big plays, when opponents kept doing enough to reach the end zone.

I ranked Canalave seventh in Week 4. A 1–5 finish and 183 total points leave the final position fifteen places lower. Weezing’s first-team selection and Passimian’s ten sacks offer something to preserve. Gabite ran for 800 yards, yet the offense seldom gave that defense much support. The offseason has a clear assignment before anyone asks for another optimistic early ranking.

The one-point finale win brings Sootopolis to 7–10, with Drampa’s 3,169 passing yards and Kingdra’s six interceptions among the useful production. Pachirisu’s retirement removes a first-team safety from a defense that already allowed 354 points. Twenty-third reflects a competitive middle with a substantial confirmed hole to fill before the next schedule begins.

Cerulean beat Sunyshore and Cinnabar, then finished with three losses. Farigiraf’s 3,532 passing yards did not receive much help from a rushing leader with 224. The defense allowed 365 points. A seven-win team has several ways to improve, and the Tide demonstrated nearly all of them by making the best results so difficult to repeat.

The offensive rookie award for Ponyta and Vigoroth’s 807 rushing yards give Veilstone a young pair worth following. They helped produce only 185 team points, so there is considerable work around them. Sandslash’s retirement adds a defensive vacancy. The Fists finish twenty-fifth with more specific offensive promise than several neighbors and too little completed scoring to climb further.

Pastoria beat two eventual division winners, Lavender and Eterna, and still closed with four losses. Kilowattrel, Banette and Dubwool had useful individual seasons. Safety Azumarill’s retirement now removes fourteen starts. Twenty-sixth reflects how little sustained offense followed those good wins; the draft needs to add dependable work around the contributors already present.

Gabite rushed for 1,126 yards and Sigilyph intercepted eleven passes. Viridian won five games. That is enough individual success to make the wider failure worth inspecting closely. The retirement of Wigglytuff and Volbeat creates two linebacker jobs immediately. Twenty-seventh leaves room for a better roster to support the players who already performed at a high level.

Oinkologne and Drakloak supplied 943 rushing and 732 receiving yards respectively, but Snowpoint lost its final five games. Medicham’s retirement adds a safety vacancy after thirteen starts. A 2–7 close-game record suggests the roster can improve its result with better late possessions. It still has to make those plays; the draft board does not award retroactive wins.

Drednaw earned first-team All-League with 11.5 sacks, and Oreburgh won its finale over Canalave. The larger season was 4–13 with nine close losses. A high first-round pick can change an important position, which is why Calvin’s quarterback projection deserves attention. It cannot by itself explain away all the possessions that kept the Miners from finishing those games.

Azalea scored 182 points, one above the league low, and lost five straight to close. Pyroar’s receiving and Zoroark’s second-team award preserve a few bright spots. The earlier close wins over Rustboro and Olivine were real. So was the offensive difficulty that followed. Thirtieth is where the full season lands after the last of those early arguments runs out.

The league’s 413 points allowed outweigh the encouraging win over Vermilion and two narrow closing division defeats. Toxapex made second-team All-League, so the defense has one recognized contributor to support. Fortree went 0–6 within the division. Better protection may help the offense; a substantial improvement in defensive reliability is necessary to move this ranking very far.

Three wins and 387 points allowed put Fuchsia last, even with Empoleon passing for 3,434 yards and Heatmor receiving 850. Seaking’s retirement creates another linebacker opening. The projected first pick offers an opportunity to add a major contributor. The Shadows will need several more good decisions around that player to make the next season feel different by November.
